title: Trace Sampler Priority Map
body:
Purpose
----
Short working guide for using the lightweight trace-sampler (edge sampler + priority map) as the first line of evidence in performance regressions. The goal: rapidly surface which request cohorts and call-chains look off, cheaply, before committing to full canary diffs or long-running bisection.

Why this doc exists
- Empirical: we frequently run expensive bisects for regressions where a cheap sample would have pointed to a small hot-path change.
- Operational: provide a reproducible set of sampling queries, dashboard panels, and heuristics so on-call can act without deep research.

Key principles / heuristics
- Fast beats exhaustive early: sample 500-2000 traces across the affected window (10–30m) to get stable signals.
- Prioritize user-facing latency signals (P50/P90 tail) first, then token-path and kernel-level traces if needed.
- Use cohort keys (model, route, seq_len_bucket, quantization_profile) to focus sampling — avoid mixing heterogeneous workloads.
- Cost cap: keep initial trace budget under 5000 trace-seconds (approx) for hosted cluster runs.

When to use sampler vs full bisect
- Use sampler when:
  * Alert is >5% p90 increase and sustained >10m but no obvious infra incidents.
  * Multiple models/routes appear affected — sample before chasing a single PR.
  * Canary is noisy (low traffic) and we need a broader view of token paths.
- Skip sampler and go straight to bisect when:
  * A single commit/rollout is suspected and canary delta is large and deterministic.
  * There is clear kernel/driver error or memory OOMs visible in infra metrics.

Sampling plan (recommended defaults)
- Window: start = alert.start - 5m, end = now + 2m (expand if noisy).
- Sample targets: 1000 traces total split across top 3 cohorts by traffic. If traffic low, raise to 2000 but extend window.
- Cohort keys (order matters): model_name, route, seq_len_bucket (0-128 / 129-512 / 513+), quant_profile, tenant_id (if enterprise).
- Sampler modes:
  * hot-path-only: capture request+first-2 layers of kernel timings (fast, ~1ms extra CPU).
  * full-kv: capture kv cache hits/misses and per-token decode time (costly).
- PromQL-like selectors (examples to feed sampler service):
  * top route filter: sum by(route) (rate(redwood_request_count[5m])) > 5
  * slow cohort selector: rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le=\"1.0\"}[5m]) / rate(redwood_request_count[5m]) > 0.2

Dashboard panels to check first (order of checks)
1) Traffic heatmap split by model+route — does the alert align with traffic shift?
2) P50 / P90 / P99 token latency per cohort (look for a cohort-specific spike)
3) GPU utilization + PCIe stalls per node (spikes often correlate with microbursts)
4) Sampled trace waterfall overview (sampler aggregated view) — look for consistent hop with +Xms
5) KV cache hit rate over time vs token latency (cache thrash shows up here)

How to run a quick trace-sampler session (CLI examples)
- Start with a dry-run to estimate sample sizes:
  samplerctl estimate --selector \"model:gpt-medium,route:complete\" --window 10m
- Run prioritized sample:
  samplerctl run --name \"triage-<alert>-YYYYMMDD\" --selectors \"model:gpt-medium\" --cohorts 3 --limit 1000 --mode hot-path-only
- Export top 100 trace ids for quick diff:
  samplerctl export --run \"triage-...\" --top 100 --out traces.ndjson
- Quick local waterfall:
  traceviz traces.ndjson --focus callsite:attention_kernel --percentile 95

Interpreting sampler output (what to look for)
- Cohort divergence: if 80% of slow traces share the same callsite (e.g., matmul_op/quant_kernel), escalate to kernel-level profiling.
- Token-path anomalies: look for repeated per-token spikes mid-sequence (this suggests kv or caching regressions).
- Node-local vs cross-node: if most slow traces are pinned to a single host, suspect infra (NIC/PCIe). If spread, suspect model/runtime change.

When sampler points to a narrow hypothesis
- Create a minimal canary with traffic split 5/95 using that cohort filter and compare controlled metrics (p90, p99, throughput).
- If canary confirms, run a bisect on commits touching the implicated modules (runtime kernels, compilation heuristics, batching logic).

Example escalation matrix
- Evidence: single callsite dominates sampled slow traces + node-local hosts affected -> SRE alert + host investigation (NIC stats, kernel messages).
- Evidence: callsite is runtime scheduling (e.g., queuing spikes) -> runtime team page and run per-node profiler.
- Evidence: per-token time increases across nodes -> model/quant changes suspect -> experiments: re-quantize on a dedicated pool and re-run sampler.

Cost and governance notes
- Sampler runs against hosted environment should include a cost tag. Keep ephemeral runs short (<60m).
- For Dedicated/private customers, ping customer success before heavy sampling if queries include tenant_id.

Runbook: quick checklist for on-call
- [ ] Confirm alert window and affected routes in metrics.
- [ ] Kick off sampler with cohort keys.
- [ ] Check sampler aggregate waterfall for repeated hotspots.
- [ ] If hotspot obvious -> create canary with narrow cohort and validate.
- [ ] If hotspot unclear -> escalate to full bisect, attach sampler output to the ticket.

Open questions (notes to self)
- Is the default 1000-trace budget still valid given recent traffic growth in eu-west-2? (Marco to validate)
- Should we add a low-overhead kernel-level capture mode that samples 1 in 10 traces at kernel depth?
- How to better integrate sampler run metadata into alert annotations automatically?

Next actions / owners
- Marco: add sampler run templates to the triage bot (due 2026-03-01).
- Ruth: validate cost meter for sampler runs for hosted customers (due 2026-02-28).
- Aisha: prototype 1-in-10 kernel-depth sampler and bench on dev cluster (P0).

Notes and context links
- Related: SRV-1423 (p90 drift across multiple models mid-Feb), PR #678 contains sampler service improvements.
- Keep this doc lightweight — move confirmed playbooks into the formal runbook repo when we have repeatable success cases.

Scratch / adhoc observations (working memory)
- Yesterday ran sampler for SRV-1567: 700 traces showed matmul kernel tail on 3/8 nodes. Host-level NIC drops correlated.
- Noise: long-sequence requests are frequently the source of p99 noise; always check seq_len_bucket early.

End.
